title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident illustrates AI-generated impersonation used as a fraud mechanism. Scammers produced a fabricated news article depicting a real public interview that never took place, using the identities of two named, recognizable Australians to lend the content credibility. The deception was not a failure of a legitimate AI deployment but a deliberate misuse of AI tools to manufacture false content at scale, combining fake articles, websites, and social media advertisements into coordinated campaigns designed to extract money and personal information from victims.

The failure mode is synthetic disinformation, specifically the use of AI to generate plausible but entirely false media artifacts that impersonate real people and real institutions. This kind of fraud is constructed outside any governed deployment pipeline, which means there is no internal checkpoint, moderation layer, or human review process that would catch it before it reaches potential victims. Detection depends entirely on third parties, regulators, or the targets themselves identifying the content as fake after it has already circulated.

What is not established is the scale of individual financial harm caused by this specific fabricated article, nor is it proven that any particular AI tool or platform was responsible for generating it. ASIC's figures describe a broad trend in scam volume and category growth, and the regulator's warning is not a finding of liability against any named party.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article depicted Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The interview never actually occurred. This fabricated story represents a growing category of scam that uses artificial intelligence to create convincing fake content featuring well-known Australians. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports that AI-generated investment scams are becoming increasingly common and sophisticated.

Last year, ASIC took down 19,400 scams overall, a 182 percent increase from the previous year. Phishing scams surged 279 percent, while fake investment platforms jumped 151 percent. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is the most frequently impersonated public figure, followed by other politicians and prominent financial personalities. Scammers build elaborate webs of deception including fake news articles, websites, and social media advertisements to lure victims into providing personal information and investing money. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing.
